title: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC)
summary: DMARC is a scalable mechanism by which a mail-originating organization can express domain-level policies and preferences for message validation, disposition, and reporting, which a receiving organization can use to improve handling of mail. This informational document was replaced by RFC 9989, RFC 9990, and RFC 9991.

eli5.summary: A company tells mail receivers what to do with messages that pretend to be from it, and asks for reports. This was replaced by RFC 9989, RFC 9990, and RFC 9991.

questions: what is the dmarc pct tag
subtitle: How a domain owner publishes in DNS what receivers should do with mail that fails authentication, and how receivers report back.

tldr.problem: SPF and DKIM can authenticate mail domains, but there was no widely accepted way for a domain to tell receivers what to do with failures, or to get feedback on how well its authentication worked.
tldr.mechanism: A domain owner publishes a DNS TXT record at the _dmarc subdomain of its domain with a policy of none, quarantine or reject. Receivers check that the RFC5322.From domain aligns with an SPF or DKIM result, apply the policy, and send aggregate and failure reports.
tldr.outcome: This Informational document was later replaced by RFC 9989, RFC 9990 and RFC 9991. It also notes that mailing lists and other mediators often break alignment and so prevent a DMARC pass.

today: RFC 7489 is an Informational, independent-stream document, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 9989, RFC 9990 and RFC 9991. It was also updated by RFC 8553 and RFC 8616.

sections.title: The Problem DMARC Addresses
sections.content:
The Sender Policy Framework (SPF) and DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) give receivers domain-level authentication. But the RFC says there was no single widely accepted mechanism for a domain to communicate its message-handling policy to receivers, or to ask for reports on how its mail was authenticated and treated. Without feedback, senders could not tell how effective their authentication was.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) lets Domain Owners and receivers collaborate in two ways: receivers get assertions about the Domain Owner's policy, and senders get feedback so they can monitor authentication and judge threats.

The outline is short. Domain Owners publish policy in the DNS. Receivers compare the RFC5322.From address with the SPF and DKIM results and the DMARC policy, decide how to handle the mail, and send reports to the Domain Owner.
sections.eli5: Before this, a company could lock its mail in a few ways but had no way to tell others what to do with fakes, or to find out how many fakes there were. DMARC adds both.

sections.title: Identifier Alignment
sections.content:
DMARC checks the domain in the RFC5322.From header, the one most mail programs show to users. A message passes only if at least one of SPF or DKIM produces a pass for an identifier that is aligned with that domain. Merely bearing a valid signature is not enough, because a message can carry a valid signature from any domain, including a mailing list or a bad actor.

Alignment can be relaxed or strict. In relaxed mode the two domains need the same Organizational Domain. For example, a DKIM d= domain of example.com aligns with a From address at news.example.com. In strict mode only an exact match counts, so that same example fails. A single message can carry several DKIM signatures, and it passes if any aligned one verifies.

The Organizational Domain is found by consulting a public suffix list and taking the matching suffix plus one more label. The RFC calls this a heuristic and says no list is guaranteed to be accurate or current.
sections.eli5: It is like checking that the name on the envelope matches the name on the stamp. Relaxed means the same family name is enough. Strict means the full name must match.

sections.title: The DMARC Policy Record
sections.content:
A Domain Owner publishes policy as a DNS TXT record at the _dmarc subdomain, for example _dmarc.example.com. The record uses the tag-value syntax from DKIM. The v tag must be first and must be DMARC1, and the p tag must follow it. Unknown tags MUST be ignored.

The main tags are:

  • p: requested policy, one of none, quarantine or reject. sp sets a different policy for subdomains.
  • adkim and aspf: r (relaxed, the default) or s (strict).
  • pct: percentage of failing mail the policy applies to, from 0 to 100, default 100, so owners can roll out slowly.
  • rua and ruf: where to send aggregate and failure reports, as a comma-separated list of URIs. Without them, receivers MUST NOT generate those reports.
  • ri: requested seconds between aggregate reports, default 86400.
  • fo: failure reporting options (0, 1, d, s).
  • rf: failure report format, default afrf.

A report URI can carry a size limit, as in mailto:reports@example.com!50m.
sections.eli5: The company writes a short note on a public board with its rules: what to do with fakes, how strict to be, and where to send the reports.

sections.title: What Receivers Do
sections.content:
A receiver extracts the From domain and queries the DNS for a DMARC record at that name. If none is found, it queries the Organizational Domain instead. Records that do not start with the right v= tag are discarded, and if multiple records or none remain, DMARC is not applied. The receiver then runs DKIM and SPF checks, tests alignment, and applies the policy to messages that fail.

Messages that fail are handled per the policy: quarantine can mean placing in a spam folder or extra scrutiny, and reject SHOULD happen during the SMTP transaction. If pct excludes a message from reject, the receiver SHOULD treat it as though quarantine applies.

Final disposition is always a matter of local policy. Receivers MAY deviate from the published policy, for example because of forwarding, and SHOULD say so through the PolicyOverride feature of the aggregate report. A policy of p=none SHOULD NOT change existing mail handling, so owners can get feedback without affecting delivery.
sections.eli5: The post office reads the rules, checks whether the letter's name matches its proof, and then follows the rules. It can still use its own judgment, as long as it tells the company.

sections.title: Aggregate and Failure Reports
sections.content:
Aggregate reports are sent daily or more often. They summarize the policy applied, the disposition, SPF and DKIM identifiers and results, alignment, and message counts. They are an XML file that SHOULD be GZIP compressed and are normally sent by email, with the format defined in Appendix C. Generators SHOULD align report periods to hour boundaries, and 24-hour reports should start at 00:00 UTC.

Failure reports are sent almost immediately after a DMARC failure and use the Abuse Reporting Format. They carry more detail about the individual message, and this RFC adds a required Identity-Alignment field. Receivers are encouraged to aggregate them, because an attacker could otherwise cause a flood of reports to a victim.

Reports may go to addresses outside the Domain Owner's control, but the receiver is meant to verify that: it looks up a TXT record at <policy domain>._report._dmarc.<destination host> that starts with v=DMARC1. If that cannot be confirmed, the URI MUST be ignored. This stops a bad actor from pointing reports at a victim.
sections.eli5: Every day the post office mails a tally of the letters it saw. For suspicious single letters, it can send a quick note right away. It first checks that the person who gets the tally agreed to receive it.

sections.title: Limits, Privacy and Security
sections.content:
DMARC deals only with exact-domain spoofing. It does not address look-alike ("cousin") domains or the human-readable display name in the From field. It also depends on SPF and DKIM, so their limits apply. Mediators such as mailing lists often break authentication or alignment and so prevent a pass.

A subdomain can also be a weak point: if someone controls the SPF record or DKIM selector for a subdomain, they can produce DMARC-passing mail for the Organizational Domain. The RFC suggests being careful about delegating subdomains and considering strict alignment.

Reports raise privacy concerns. Failure reports can expose full message content, and both report types can expose sender and recipient addresses. The RFC encourages secure transport for reports and recommends deploying DNSSEC, since DMARC depends on the security of the DNS. When rejecting during SMTP, it suggests including the word "DMARC" in the reply text.
sections.eli5: The sign only helps against letters that copy the exact name. Lookalike names and tricky nicknames still get past it, and the reports themselves can contain private things, so they must be handled with care.

items.label: No specific action
items.desc: The Domain Owner requests no specific action on delivery; it SHOULD NOT change existing mail handling.

items.label: Treat as suspicious
items.desc: Failing mail is treated as suspicious, for example placed in a spam folder or flagged.

items.label: Reject the mail
items.desc: Failing mail should be rejected, preferably during the SMTP transaction.
